title: Count plans with a table

blocks.text: The port authority's real list has 60 candidate repairs, so checking all $`2^{60}`$ subsets is out of the question. It still wants to know how many subsets fit the budget, as a lower bound on its open plans when only the budget touches those repairs.

Write `count_within(costs, budget)` in `within.py`: the number of subsets of the projects (the empty one included) whose total cost is at most `budget`. Costs and the budget are whole numbers, costs are positive.

Use a table, not a list of subsets. Let `ways[b]` be the number of subsets of the projects seen so far that cost exactly `b`, for every `b` from 0 to the budget. Before any project, `ways[0] = 1` (the empty subset) and every other entry is 0. A project of cost `c` updates the table with
\text{ways}[b] \mathrel{+}= \text{ways}[b - c] \qquad \text{for } b \text{ from the budget down to } c
The answer is the sum of the final table. Work out why the loop must run downward before you write it. About six lines.

"""Run executes this file. Change the calls and see what prints. Submit grades."""
import logging

# Turn the logger up, so the `log.debug` lines of your code show under the printed lines.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

from within import count_within

print("costs [25, 35, 50] within 60:", count_within([25, 35, 50], 60))
print("costs [25, 35, 50] within 110:", count_within([25, 35, 50], 110))
print("costs [5, 10, 15, 20] within 25:", count_within([5, 10, 15, 20], 25))
print("no costs within 10:", count_within([], 10))

    print(count_within([30, 40], 70))
